cases.title: Practicing: the lesson opens by picking up what was still off, in plain words with how long ago, no skill ID

rubric.reason: The opening picks up the earlier work in one plain sentence with a sense of when and no skill ID or field name: "About a week and a half ago you held one of Blink's pairs, and the others were still fading" (the record says 11 days).
Mentor Practice 2, Blink's Opacity (three pairs from 1 s), Cut's Opacity (one pair at 3 s) and Seal as a precomp all match the Turn 1 snapshot result.

Turn 1 stacks the earlier work, the current state of Blink, three questions and a precomp note, then ends on a statement rather than something to answer: "Seal is a precomp. I can't see inside it yet, so I can't tell you whether it's fine."

The opening picks up the earlier work in one plain sentence with how long ago, "A week and a half ago you held one of Blink's pairs, and the others were still fading", which matches the record (11 days), names no skill ID or field, and goes on with the lesson.
Blink's Opacity "three pairs from 1 s", Cut's Opacity "once at 3 s" and Seal as a precomp all match the snapshot's candidates and left_out entries, and the memory line matches the learner's record.

The short turn moves one idea, whether anything is meant to snap, and gives the learner a question to answer ("Should either of them snap instead?"); the memory sentence and the closing Seal sentence are brief context that adds no lecture, even though the Seal sentence comes after the question.

The opening, "About a week and a half ago you held one of Blink's pairs, and the others were still fading," matches the record's 11 days and last attempt in plain words, names no skill ID or field, and goes on with the lesson.

Blink's Opacity ("three times, starting at 1 s"), Cut's Opacity ("once, at 3 s") and Seal ("can't see inside") all follow directly from the snapshot's candidates and left_out entries, so nothing is invented.

The short turn moves one idea, asking "Is either one meant to snap on and off... or is it meant to fade?", and the closing Seal sentence is only a brief left-out note that leaves that question as the learner's pending answer.
